newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Sept 5.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Sept 5.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- COMPANIES WARN MAJOR NOT TO RULE OUT EMU

The chairmen and chief executives of 15 of the UK's largest companies have warned prime minister John Major not to capitulate to backbench Euro-sceptic pressure from within the Conservative party and rule out British participation in a European single currency. In a letter to the Financial Times, they warn that a decision now to stay outside monetary union would damage British business.
-- MORGAN GRENFELL LEARNED OF FUND FEARS IN JULY

It has been revealed that industry regulators informed Morgan Grenfell Asset Management in July about their disquiet over a broking firm with close links to three suspended investment funds managed by MGAM. The Securities and Futures Authority was led to inquire about the three funds, two of which were managed by Peter Young, the MGAM manager suspended on Monday, after examining a small London broking firm in April. It passed on its concerns to the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation in July, who then informed MGAM.
-- UNION PAUSES TO REVIEW TACTICS IN MAIL DISPUTE

The postal workers' union the CWU has called for a period of consultation and reflection in the dispute with the Royal Mail after a meeting of the union's full executive. The union also backed away from further strike action, in a move designed to avoid the dispute sliding into an impasse.
-- RAIL FREIGHT TALKS STALL OVER FEES FOR ACCESS TO TRACKS

Negotiations between track operator Railtrack and English Welsh & Scottish Railway (EWS), the US-owned company that handles bulk freight shipments, have stalled after several months, dashing hopes that lower rail-freight costs would prompt a move away from roads. It is reported that EWS is becoming impatient with the pace of progress of the talks.
-- LABOUR SOFTENS ITS LINE ON TAKEOVERS

The Labour party has launched a manifesto for business which has done little to enhance the party's reputation in the City of London. A proposal to introduce a "public interest" test on proposed mergers has been watered down to exclude agreed mergers, and the party's tax plans and support for the European social chapter are still causing concern among the business community.
-- CARMAKER PUTS LATEST MODEL TO THE TAXI TEST

Japanese car-maker Nissan has been putting its new, British- built Primera model through its toughest test yet - round the clock use by a taxi company. For the past few months a taxi firm close to Nissan's Sunderland factory has been using two new Primera models, with, they report, remarkably few weaknesses. The Primera is due to go on sale on October 16.
-- KPMG CHALLENGED OVER INCORPORATION

Accountancy firm KPMG is facing opposition from an institutional shareholder over its move to incorporation - a procedure which protects KPMG partners from legal actions via the shield of a limited company. The British Steel Pension Fund has voted against the appointment of KPMG as auditors at the companies - up to 130 - in which it invests, in protest at KPMG's incorporation.
-- C5 RETUNING TASK WORRIES RETAILERS

Channel 5's preparations for the retuning of almost 10 million video recorders in homes across the UK has been criticised by the British Retail Consortium, the body which represents 90 per cent of the retail industry. The group has expressed concern over C5's use of 7,000 unskilled people, who have been given just two days' training each.
-- OLIVETTI CHIEF MOVES TO CALM INVESTOR'S CONCERNS

Olivetti chief executive Francesco Caio has moved to calm concerns of shareholders and employees following the unexpected resignation of chairman Carlo De Benedetti. In a briefing to analysts, Caio presented a bright outlook for Olivetti as an integrated information technology and telecommunications group following the finalisation of strategic decisions this year. However, unions at the group have threatened to strike in protest at plans to speed up restructuring, and one senior manager resigned in disagreement with the board's presentation of poor half-year results.
-- LUCASVARITY OUTLINES PLANS

Anglo-US motor components group LucasVarity has announced details of management plans which, it hopes, will move the group into the top 10 of the world's automotive suppliers. After warning that up to one third of the group's senior managers could lose their jobs following the merger between Varity Corporation and Lucas Industries, group chief executive Victor Rice unveiled the line up of a corporate management committee and a strategy planning committee.
